job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Wendy Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at 6:30 and in the office at Dunbar Hardware Supply by 8:00. It's a family-owned wholesaler in Ferris Cross that sells to builders and shops. I'm the payroll and accounts clerk, so I run wages for 31 people, match invoices and send reminders to late payers. I like that everyone knows everyone. I rent a room with Ruth, a friend from church, and on Wednesdays I sing in the choir. My student loan is 39,000, which my parents don't know the half of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I never believed the fuss. At work I'd tell Mr. Dunbar, the owner, that our books still need a person who knows the families and the suppliers. At church I'd say the same, that real work still needs real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel relieved, but I'd still be counting pennies. I earn 22,500, Ruth and I pay 420 each for the house, and the loan takes 190 a month. There are only two other firms around here that need payroll clerks, so I can't be picky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and ask Mr. Dunbar for a small rise after my first year. I'd put 40 a month aside for the wedding fund, as Tom (my fiancé) and I want to marry in about three years. I'd keep singing and I'd go to the apprenticeship evening at the college, to see if they run an accounting route that I can do alongside work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I suppose. Quiet. It's the kind of life I thought I'd have, though the loan is a weight I carry every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your parents don't know the half of the loan. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they worked hard to give me everything and they'd worry. Dad drives a delivery van and Mum does hours at a school canteen. They believe university was the safe route, and I don't want to tell them the loan is bigger than their yearly pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help most with the loan, if nothing else changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper job that pays more, that's all. I don't want handouts. I'd like employers to train people and pay fairly. I'd also like a loan that doesn't grow faster than I can pay it off.

I'd tell Mr. Dunbar (the owner) that our books still need a **person** who knows the families.
think: I'm relieved but **counting pennies**: 22,500 pay, 420 rent and 190 a month to the loan.

Go to the college **apprenticeship** evening and ask about an accounting route.
feel: **Settled** and quiet, like the life I expected, with the loan as a daily weight.

fieldNote: Hides the size of her **loan** from her parents out of pride and care.

Favours **work** and training over support, in line with her traditional outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't like it, and I'd say it plainly. Machines doing the checking and booking sounds like less work for ordinary people. At work I'd tell Mr. Dunbar I can do the job by hand and do it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think payroll is one of the things that goes. Wages, invoices, reminders, it's all on the card. Mr. Dunbar won't want to let go of a loyal clerk, but he might not replace me if I left. I don't use these tools and I'd rather not start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing everything by hand and make myself the one who knows every account and every family. If he bought a payroll program, I'd learn it, but slowly. I'd talk to the pastor and the choir about work, in case someone knows of something. And I'd keep saving the 40 a month and put off any big spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unhappy. It's not the sort of change I asked for. It feels like something done to people, rather than for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not start with the tools. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust them. I've heard of them getting numbers wrong, and I'd be the one in trouble. Also I don't like how people talk to them like friends. I'm not against progress, but I'd like it to prove itself first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Dunbar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Sheila in the warehouse office. She's 58, she does the stock cards by hand, and she's three years from a pension. If they bring in a system, I'd want Mr. Dunbar to keep her on. I'd say it to his face if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is terrifying, and the people running things haven't said a word about families. I'd say we should look after our own: neighbours, church, local firms. I'd say it plainly at church and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my work is gone, and the work of everyone I know on a desk. Mr. Dunbar will keep the firm going, but with a computer and one person instead of five. I've got 39,000 of debt, three weeks of savings and a wedding I'd want to afford. I'd feel I did what I was told and it still went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents and Tom's family if I could live with them to cut rent. I'd put the wedding off and use that money against the loan. I'd look for any hands-on work with people, like a care home or the school canteen where Mum works, because machines come later there. I'd go to church on Wednesday and talk to the pastor about help. And I'd ask Mr. Dunbar what's coming, straight out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, like a child lost in a shop. I'd feel I should have seen it and I didn't. And I'd feel ashamed of being afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the wedding off. How would Tom take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be hurt first, then he'd understand. He's an electrician's apprentice, so he's safer than me for now. We'd probably marry small instead of waiting, with the church hall and no fuss. I'd rather be married and poor than single and poor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth about the loan, finally. It would be hard, but if I'm moving home I can't hide it. Dad would probably go quiet, and Mum would cry and then feed me. That's how they are.

say: Two years is **terrifying**, and nobody in charge has mentioned families.
We should look after our own: **neighbours**, church and local firms.
think: My work is **gone**, and Mr. Dunbar will run the firm with a computer and one person.
With 39,000 of debt and three weeks saved, I did what I was told and it still went **wrong**.

Use the wedding money against the **loan** and look for care or canteen work.
Talk to the **pastor** and ask Mr. Dunbar what's coming.
feel: **Scared**, like a child lost in a shop, and ashamed of being afraid.
S2.quote: I'd rather be married and poor than single and poor.
fieldNote: Falls back on **family** and church rather than politics or protest.
Will finally tell her **parents** the truth about the loan.
Plans to marry **smaller** and sooner rather than wait, a family-first choice.

steps.text: Ask my parents or Tom's family if I can live with them

Put the wedding money against the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to get ready if we don't waste it. I'd say people should learn a skill that needs hands and hearts, and families should save. And I'd tell the government to back apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm worried but not hopeless. In five years I could be married, have the loan down to half, and be doing something steadier than payroll. But it's the sort of thing where I'd always be looking over my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an accounting apprenticeship at the college this year, if Mr. Dunbar lets me do it on day release. I'd also get good at the tasks that stay human, like talking to customers about late invoices. I'd keep saving 60 a month, and Tom and I would marry in the second year. If the firm let me go, I'd look at the school office or a care home admin job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a sense that I can do something. It's better than waiting for a storm without a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an accounting apprenticeship still make sense if AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, and I'd be honest about that. But I'd rather learn something than do nothing. And the people who sign things off will still need to be trusted, which is a human thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tom think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says we'll manage. He's got a trade, so he believes it will be fine. I'm not as sure, but I like that he's steady. We'd both be working for the same small house.

I'd tell the government to back **apprenticeships**, not handouts.
think: I'm worried but not **hopeless**: married, loan halved and doing something steadier than payroll.
I'd always be looking over my **shoulder**.

fieldNote: The longer window turns her fear into a **plan** built around apprenticeship.
Relies on **Tom's** trade for confidence but isn't fully convinced.
Gets her **sense** of safety from trust and people, not tech.

steps.text: Start an accounting apprenticeship at the college on day release

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent warning, and we should use it to teach skills and build up local jobs. I'd say it at church and at work, calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, as long as I stayed useful. By 32 I could have paid the loan, be married with a child, and be in a steadier job. The worry is I'd be the sort who waits too long. I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Dunbar for a couple of years and finish the apprenticeship. I'd marry Tom in about three years and save for a house, maybe in Ferris Cross near my parents. I'd learn the payroll software when the firm brings it in, not before. I'd keep up with church and keep saving 80 a month once the loan's lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite peaceful, honestly. With ten years you could have a family and a house and a plan. It'd feel like normal life, with a little cloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the little cloud?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my generation might have a worse time than my parents. They had one job all their life. I might have three or four, and a machine looking over each one. I don't know if that's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children to study something different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade and a bit of everything else. A degree alone didn't protect me, as I found. I'd want them to have something they can do with their hands and something they can do with their heads.

say: Ten years is a decent **warning**; use it to teach skills and build local jobs.
I'd say it calmly at church and at **work**.
think: I'd be fine if I stayed **useful**, married with a child and the loan paid by 32.
I'm the sort who waits **too long**, and I know it.

Marry Tom in about three years and save for a **house** near my parents.

S4.quote: A degree alone didn't protect me, as I found.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** to new tools shows in learning only when required.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'm not quick with change, and I'd have no time to find my feet. What would help is jobs for people who aren't clever with computers, apprenticeships and employers who keep people on instead of dropping them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people say young people want handouts. We don't. We want a fair chance to work and look after our families, and we want the work to still be there.

headlineQuote: We want a fair chance to work and look after our families, and we want the work to still be there.
portrait: **Wendy** is 22, an accounting graduate working as a payroll clerk at a family wholesaler in Ferris Cross, renting with a friend.
She owes **39,000**, has about three weeks of savings and hasn't told her parents the full amount.
She is traditional, church-going and engaged, favours **work** and apprenticeships over handouts, and never uses AI.
She turns to family, church and **hands-on** care work as fear rises, and to apprenticeships when there's time.
Time lets her plan a **wedding**, a house and children; two years leaves her alarmed.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because she changes slowly and would have no time to find her feet.
whatWouldHelp: **Jobs** for people who aren't comfortable with computers, apprenticeships and employers who keep staff.
